617.title: As light belongs to the sun
617.hook: Ravana offers Sita his kingdom, and she answers through a blade of grass
617.carry: sita and ram, never apart, like light and sun
617.howItsDone: Sita's blade of grass appears in Hindu storytelling and devotional art, and many Hindus chant 'Sita Ram' or greet one another with 'Jai Siya Ram', naming Sita first.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashoka, the grove called without sorrow, and Sita in it. Your line: the light within is covered, never put out.
screen: `THE LIGHT WITHIN IS COVERED, NEVER PUT OUT.`

segments.voice: Hanuman is still hidden in the tree, working out how to approach Sita, when the garden fills with light and noise. Night is ending. Torches. Music. Ravana is coming, surrounded by his queens, walking straight toward the woman Hanuman just found. Hanuman makes himself even smaller in the leaves and holds perfectly still. And Sita, seeing who it is, pulls her knees up and wraps her arms around herself.
screen: `TORCHES BEFORE DAWN.` → `RAVANA COMES TO THE GROVE.` → `SITA DRAWS IN.`

segments.voice: Ravana speaks first, a long, smooth speech. He praises her beauty. He offers her everything: his kingdom, his wealth, the place of chief queen above all his wives. Forget Rama, he says, a beggar in the forest; you'll never see him again. Before Sita answers, she places a blade of grass between herself and him. In Sanskrit, tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā: putting a blade of grass in between. Readers take it several ways: that she won't face him directly, that he's worth no more to her than grass, that even grass is a wall he cannot cross. Valmiki doesn't explain; he lets her do it. Then her words: I am no more apart from Rama than light is from the sun. Give me back to him, if you want to live. Ravana gives her two months, then storms off, and Hanuman, hidden in the branches, has heard every word. Hold on to her image, because Hindus never let it go. Light isn't added to the sun; it is the sun, shining. That's how the tradition sees Sita and Rama: not a hero and his prize, but one divine pair, so close you can't say one name without the other. It's why people chant Sita-Ram as if it were one word, and why so many greet each other with Jai Siya Ram, Sita's name first. Many teachers go further and call Sita Rama's own shakti, his power: the light of the sun itself.
screen: `RAVANA OFFERS EVERYTHING.` · `A BLADE OF GRASS BETWEEN THEM.` · `LIGHT AND SUN, NEVER APART.` · then, large: `SITA-RAM, ONE NAME.`

618.title: Wherever Rama's story is told
618.hook: Hanuman finds a way to reach a frightened Sita: he tells her Rama's story
618.carry: where rama's story is told, hanuman listens
618.howItsDone: Before a Ramayana or Sundara Kanda reading, many Hindus recite a verse saying Hanuman is present wherever Rama's glory is sung, and some families set out an empty seat for him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a blade of grass between Sita and Ravana, and your line: Sita and Ram, never apart, like light and sun.

Ravana has gone. The guards have finished threatening her and drawn back. Sita sits alone at the foot of the tree, worn out, close to the end of hope. Hanuman is right above her. He has found her, and now he faces a delicate problem. A monkey suddenly dropping out of a tree and talking, in the middle of the enemy's garden, could terrify her. If she cries out, the guards wake, and everything is lost.
screen: `SITA, ALONE, NEAR THE END OF HOPE.` → `HANUMAN, RIGHT ABOVE HER.` → `ONE CRY AND IT'S LOST.`

segments.voice: So once again Valmiki lets us hear Hanuman think. If I speak polished Sanskrit, like a learned priest, she'll think I'm Ravana in disguise; Ravana fooled her once already, dressed as a holy man. So I'll use plain, everyday speech. And I won't start with myself. I'll start with Rama. Softly, from the branches, he begins to tell a story, as if to no one. There was a king called Dasharatha, righteous and great. His eldest son Rama was sent into the forest with his wife and his brother. In the forest, his wife Sita was carried off. Rama searched for her, made friends with the monkey king Sugriva, and sent monkeys everywhere to find her. And I crossed the ocean, and I have seen her. That's all. The first thing she hears is her husband's name, and Sita lifts her head. Notice what Hanuman is doing up there: telling Rama's story to someone in sorrow. Hindus have done it ever since. Families read the Ramayana aloud in hard times, and a Sundara Kanda path, a reading of this very book, is a common way to pray. And there's a loved belief about who is listening. A verse many recite before a reading says: wherever Rama's glory is sung, Hanuman is there, palms joined above his head, eyes full of tears. So at many readings a seat is kept empty for him. Hanuman was the first to tell Rama's story in Lanka. Hindus believe he never stopped listening.

619.title: Describe him to me
619.hook: Sita sees a monkey in the branches and wonders if she's dreaming, then remembers she hasn't slept
619.carry: dhyana: see the form you love, detail by detail
619.howItsDone: Hanuman's description of Rama is among the best-loved passages of the Sundara Kanda, and many Hindus begin worship with a dhyana verse that describes the deity's form before the prayer itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita found. Hanuman told Rama's story softly from the tree, and your line: where Rama's story is told, Hanuman listens.

Sita hears her own story drifting down from the tree. She looks up into the leaves and sees a small monkey, pale gold, with bright eyes, sitting among the white blossoms. When something you've wanted for a very long time suddenly happens, the first feeling often isn't joy. It's disbelief. And Valmiki says her first thought is: I must be dreaming.
screen: `A SMALL MONKEY IN THE LEAVES.` → `FIRST COMES DISBELIEF.` → `I MUST BE DREAMING.`

segments.voice: Then she catches herself, and her reasoning is lovely. You can't dream unless you sleep, she thinks, and since Rama was taken from me, I haven't slept. So this is real, or it's my own longing taking shape. Hanuman climbs down slowly, bows, and joins his palms. Who are you? he asks gently. If you are Sita, the wife of Rama, tell me. She tells her own story: daughter of Janaka, wife of Rama, taken by Ravana. Then Hanuman says: I am Rama's messenger. But how can she trust a stranger who appears out of a tree in Ravana's garden? Anyone could know Rama's name. So Sita asks him to describe Rama. Not his name. Him. And Valmiki gives Hanuman a long, loving portrait: Rama's eyes, his voice, his shoulders, his walk, his steadiness, his kindness. Detail by detail, Rama comes into the grove, and her joy, still half fear, begins to grow. This is how Hindus pray, too. Before worship, many recite a dhyana verse, a verse for seeing: it paints the god from head to foot, the color, the face, what each hand holds, so the mind can hold the form before the prayer begins. Hanuman's portrait works the same way. He doesn't argue Sita into trust. He makes Rama visible, and her heart recognizes him.
screen: `NO DREAMS WITHOUT SLEEP.` · `DESCRIBE RAMA TO ME.` · `DETAIL BY DETAIL, RAMA ARRIVES.` · then, large: `DHYANA: SEEING THE FORM.`

segments.voice: If you pray, picture Rama, or the deity in your home shrine, the way Hanuman described him: start with the face and the eyes, then the shoulders, the hands and what they hold, down to the feet. One detail on each breath. If you don't pray, picture someone you love who is far away the same way, their voice, their walk, one thing they always do, and notice how close the details bring them.

620.title: The ring with Rama's name
620.hook: Rama's ring, carried across the ocean, reaches Sita's hand
620.carry: rama's name carries the devotee across the ocean
620.howItsDone: Hanuman presenting Rama's ring to Sita is a familiar scene in Ramayana painting and sculpture, and the Hanuman Chalisa remembers the ring in a line many Hindus know by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman painted Rama for Sita, and your line was dhyana: see the form you love, detail by detail.

Back in Kishkindha, the monkey armies set off in four directions, search party after search party. Rama gave only one of them a token for Sita: his own ring, engraved with his name. He gave it to Hanuman. Valmiki says Rama could see that the monkey king trusted Hanuman above all, and that Hanuman would be the one to succeed. Everyone else went searching. Hanuman went searching with a ring in his keeping.
screen: `FOUR ARMIES, FOUR DIRECTIONS.` → `ONE RING, ONE SEARCHER.`

segments.voice: Now, under the shimshapa tree, Hanuman brings it out. Look, my lady: this ring, marked with Rama's name. I've brought it so you'll believe me. Sita takes the ring in her hands, and Valmiki says she is as happy as if she had met her husband himself. Her face shines like the moon slipping free of an eclipse. Words can be faked. But this is Rama's own ring, the one she knew on his hand. Think what it has been through: forests, Svayamprabha's dark cave, a hundred yojanas of sea, past Mainaka, past Surasa's mouth, through Simhika, over Lanka's wall and up a tree. And Hindus have never forgotten it. The Hanuman Chalisa, the hymn so many Hindus know by heart, gives it a line: keeping the Lord's ring in his mouth, he leapt the ocean, and no wonder. Why no wonder? Many teachers read it this way: Hanuman didn't cross on strength alone. He carried Rama's name with him. Hindus speak of life itself as an ocean, bhavasagara, the ocean of becoming, and of the Lord's name as what carries a devotee across. That's why people write Shri Ram at the top of a page, say it before a journey, whisper it when they're afraid. The ring that reached Sita is a promise: hold his name, and the sea can be crossed.
screen: `MARKED WITH RAMA'S NAME.` · `A RING THAT CROSSED THE SEA.` · `THE RING IN THE HANUMAN CHALISA.` · then, large: `THE NAME CARRIES YOU ACROSS.`

621.title: Nectar mixed with poison
621.hook: Sita asks how Rama really is, and Hanuman's honest answer is sweet and bitter at once
621.carry: viraha: the ache of missing is love too
621.howItsDone: Devotional readings of the Sundara Kanda dwell on Rama's grief and on Sita's phrase 'nectar mixed with poison', and many bhajans sing of viraha, the longing of separation, as love itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ring with Rama's name. Sita held it as if she'd met him, and your line was: Rama's name carries the devotee across the ocean.

Sita has the ring in her hand, and now she asks the questions anyone asks about someone far away. Not the news. The person. Is Rama well? Does he still think of me? Has his love grown cold with distance? When a friend comes back from seeing someone you love, those are the questions that come first.
screen: `IS RAMA WELL?` → `DOES HE STILL THINK OF ME?`

segments.voice: Hanuman answers honestly, and his answer is a portrait of a man in grief. Rama can barely sleep. When he wakes, the first word out of him is Sita. He doesn't notice the insects that land on him. When he sees a lovely flower, he sighs and says her name. He is wasting away with sorrow, Hanuman says, but he is preparing, and he is coming. Now listen to how Sita receives it. What you've told me, she says, is nectar mixed with poison. Nectar, because Rama hasn't forgotten her; every detail of his grief proves his love. Poison, because the man she loves is suffering, and she can't reach him. Hindu devotion has a name for this ache: viraha, love in separation. And it doesn't treat the ache as a problem to fix. It honors it as one of the deepest forms of love there is. The gopis of Vrindavan, longing for Krishna after he leaves, are its great example, and Mirabai's songs are full of it. Many teachers say longing for God is already a kind of meeting, because you can only miss what you love. Rama and Sita, an ocean apart, each saying the other's name, are viraha in its plainest form. That's why a bhajan can be sad and happy at once, and why people cry while singing one and call it sweet.
screen: `RAMA WAKES SAYING SITA.` · `NECTAR MIXED WITH POISON.` · `VIRAHA: LOVE IN SEPARATION.` · then, large: `YOU CAN ONLY MISS WHAT YOU LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you miss, near or far, or gone. If you pray, offer the missing itself, the way bhajans do, with two names on the breath: Sita as you breathe in, Ram as you breathe out. If you don't pray, simply let the ache be there, and notice the love inside it: sweet and bitter in one cup, neither canceling the other.
The ring. The token that opens Sita's questions about Rama, and Hanuman's honest answer, which Sita calls nectar mixed with poison.

622.title: Why hasn't Rama come?
622.hook: Sita asks two hard questions out loud, and neither one is scolded
622.carry: the avatar's promise: when dharma falls, he comes
622.howItsDone: Some readers point to Sita's questions to Hanuman as signs of her strength, and many Hindus recite the Gita's 'yada yada hi dharmasya' verse as God's promise to come when dharma declines.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita called Hanuman's news nectar mixed with poison. Your line: viraha, the ache of missing is love too.
screen: `VIRAHA: THE ACHE OF MISSING IS LOVE TOO.`

segments.voice: People sometimes imagine Sita as endlessly patient, never questioning, never afraid. Valmiki's Sita is braver than that: she doubts out loud. A woman who has been tricked once, terribly, by someone in disguise, doesn't trust easily. A woman who has waited this long for rescue is allowed to ask why it hasn't come. Valmiki gives her both doubts, and doesn't scold her for either.
screen: `NOT ENDLESSLY PATIENT.` → `SHE DOUBTS OUT LOUD.` → `TWO DOUBTS, NO SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: The first doubt comes the moment Hanuman climbs down toward her. Sita shrinks back. What if this is Ravana again, in a new disguise, the way he once came to her hut dressed as a holy man? She says it to his face. Then she checks her own heart: when I look at you, my mind is glad. Would it be glad if you were Ravana? So she asks to hear about Rama, and she listens. The second doubt comes after the ring, and it's sharper. If Rama loves me, why hasn't he come? He and Lakshmana are mighty archers. It's the question of everyone who has waited for help that's slow, and Valmiki lets her ask it. Hanuman doesn't scold her. He answers: Rama doesn't know where you are. The moment I tell him, he'll come. For Hindus, that answer reaches far past Lanka. Rama is honored as an avatar of Vishnu, God come down into the world. And in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna, another avatar, makes the promise himself: whenever dharma declines and wrong rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good. So Hindus can ask Sita's question out loud, why haven't you come yet, and it isn't a failure of faith. Sita asked it. The answer she got wasn't a rebuke. It was: he's on his way.
screen: `WHAT IF YOU'RE RAVANA AGAIN?` · `WHY HASN'T RAMA COME?` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW WHERE YOU WERE.` · then, large: `WHEN DHARMA FALLS, HE COMES.`

segments.voice: If you pray, bring the thing you're waiting on to God plainly, the way Sita asked: why not yet? Then rest for a few breaths in the Gita's promise: whenever dharma falls, I come. If you don't pray, name what you're waiting for honestly, without pretending you're not tired of waiting, and let each out-breath be a little more patient than the last.
Her doubt. Sita's fear that Hanuman is Ravana in disguise, and her question of why Rama hasn't come: two doubts, honestly asked, and answered without a rebuke.
Your line: the avatar's promise, when dharma falls, he comes. Tomorrow, a rescue offered on the spot. Day six hundred twenty-two.

623.title: Not carried off in secret
623.hook: Hanuman offers to carry Sita home tonight, and she says no, for reasons worth hearing
623.carry: maryada: the right way matters, not just the rescue
623.howItsDone: Sita's refusal to be carried away by Hanuman is a discussed passage; many Hindu tellings read it as dignity and maryada, and Rama is widely praised as Maryada Purushottam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: her doubt. Was he Ravana in disguise? Why hadn't Rama come? Your line: the avatar's promise, when dharma falls, he comes.

It seems like the obvious ending. The rescuer is here; the captive is right in front of him. Hanuman says it out loud: climb on my back, my lady. I'll carry you across the sea today, and you'll see Rama. In a different kind of story, that would be the last page. Sita looks at the small monkey in front of her, and her first reaction is a doubt so practical it's almost funny.
screen: `CLIMB ON MY BACK.` → `ACROSS THE SEA TODAY.` → `A VERY PRACTICAL DOUBT.`

segments.voice: You're so small, she says. How could you carry me across the ocean? So Hanuman shows her. He grows, right there in the grove, until he stands like a mountain, blazing. Sita believes him now. And still she says no. Valmiki gives her reasons, and each one is real. First, the journey: high over the sea at that speed, she's afraid she'd lose her grip and fall. Second, the rakshasas would chase them, and Hanuman would have to fight while carrying her. Third, she will not willingly touch any man but Rama. Ravana seized her by force; that she couldn't help. She won't choose it now. And fourth, the one she lingers on: let Rama come, defeat Ravana and take me home himself. To be carried off in secret would be unworthy of him. Readers weigh these reasons differently. But notice: her doubt about Hanuman's size was settled in a moment. The refusal was a decision. Hindus have a word for what she is guarding: maryada, the right limits, the proper way of doing things. Rama is loved as Maryada Purushottam, the best of men, who keeps them. Sita keeps them too, even as a captive. Ravana stole her in secret; she won't be stolen back the same way. In this story, how a thing is done is part of whether it is dharma.
screen: `YOU'RE SO SMALL. HE GROWS.` · `FALLING, FIGHTING, TOUCH.` · `LET RAMA COME HIMSELF.` · then, large: `MARYADA: THE RIGHT WAY.`

segments.voice: Call up a shortcut someone has offered you, or one you've been tempted by. If you pray, hold it before Rama, Maryada Purushottam, and ask quietly: is this the right way, or just a way? If you don't pray, name its risks, one with each breath, the way Sita named hers. Then ask what the slower, cleaner way would protect. There's no need to decide yet.
Her doubt. Sita's doubt that a small monkey could carry her, settled when Hanuman grows, and her refusal, for safety, for her own choice and for Rama's honor.
Your line: maryada, the right way matters, not just the rescue. Tomorrow, the monkey who crossed an ocean calls himself the smallest. That's the week.
